reviews.detailed_mathematical_reasoning: The componentwise inclusion lemma is correct: if every root only gains incidences, every old transversal still hits every root, so tau cannot increase; deletion cannot decrease tau. From a protected state, an addition can fail the band only by lowering tau to at most 2, and a deletion can fail it only by raising tau to at least 5, apart from deletion-floor legality. Applying monotonicity to the post-state of a second candidate gives all four signs: Add->Add and Del->Del cannot turn an illegal candidate legal; Add->Del and Del->Add cannot turn a legal candidate illegal. The arguments include same-root floor effects because a same-root addition cannot reduce deletion slack and a same-root deletion cannot create it. For different roots, syntax and floor status of the receiving candidate are unchanged, so any nonzero response is mediated by the global transversal constraint. The four supplied controls are valid: two additions jointly create a pair cover, a deletion restores addition legality, two deletions jointly produce five singleton roots, and an addition restores deletion legality. Root/label permutations preserve incidence, floors carried with roots, tau, move syntax, and the response difference, so the response graph is covariant and S/F/Q/M are invariant counts.

reviews.detailed_mathematical_reasoning: The core dual-field mathematics is correct after the domain is stated precisely. For nonempty roots and |P| >= 2, W_E(K)=0 is exactly the statement that K is a two-label cover, so absence of pair covers is equivalent to tau >= 3; any cover of size 0 or 1 can be extended to a pair. A small cover H of size at most 4 is exactly the condition tau <= 4. The addition and deletion indicator updates for W are exact, with changed-coordinate counts |P|-|E_i|-1 and |P|-|E_i| respectively. Upper-cover indicators are monotone: additions cannot destroy covers and create one only when the edited root was the unique missed root; deletions cannot create covers and destroy one exactly when the edited root was hit only by x. Thus, from a protected state, additions can violate only the lower condition, while deletions can violate only the upper condition plus the local floor. The one-update bounds, witness-reservoir interpretation, and relabeling covariance follow. However, the proof opens with an unrestricted 'finite root state on palette P' and states the tau>=3 equivalence while only giving a later parenthetical 'when |P|>=2'; it never makes |P|>=2 and nonempty roots explicit standing hypotheses. For |P|=1, the universal quantifier over pairs is vacuous while tau>=3 is false for an ordinary nonempty-root hitting system, so the stated unrestricted equivalence is not literally valid. A protected finite state normally forces a sufficiently large palette (indeed |P|>=3 under the standard nonempty-root convention), but that implication and the positive-root-floor assumption must be written into the proof rather than left implicit. This is a proof-domain defect, not a failure of the update identities on the intended domain.

Palette size 1 exposes the omitted domain hypothesis: pair quantification is empty but tau>=3 is false. Roots containing all palette labels give zero changed W coordinates on addition and |P|-|E_i|=0 on deletion, consistent with the formulas. Covers of sizes 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 are included by the C definition; the pair equivalence needs the explicit extension hypothesis. Multiple covers can be created or destroyed by one incidence, and the proof correctly does not treat N4 as a conserved scalar. Empty-root behavior is not specified by the reviewed source; a positive-root-floor/nonempty-root convention must therefore be made explicit before claiming an unrestricted equivalence.

reviews.detailed_mathematical_reasoning: The construction matches all required local/global inputs. In both states the palette is {a,b,c,d,e}, there are six original roots with floor 1, R0={d}, and candidate f=Add(R0,b). Since d occurs nowhere else, the candidate root is an isolated singleton overlap component, so every finite-radius overlap view and the complete component are identical. In state L, d is forced by R0, a by singleton R3, and c or e by R2, so tau>=3; {a,c,d} covers all roots, so tau=3. In state I, d, b, and c are forced by the three singleton requirements R0, R4, R5, and {b,c,d} covers, so tau=3. After f in L, any pair must contain a for R3 and then b or d for R0; either choice misses R2={c,e}, while {a,b,c} covers, so tau remains 3 and f is legal. After f in I, {b,c} covers all roots, so tau<=2; R4={b} and R5={c} are disjoint singleton roots, so tau is exactly 2 and f is illegal. For K={b,c}, the candidate removes the sole witness R0 in I but leaves at least R0 and R3 as witnesses in L. Therefore no uniform exact legality function can use only the candidate component plus the matched palette size, root count, floors, current tau, and candidate identity/type. This is an incidence-overlap no-go, not a physical nonlocality theorem.
